cards.heading: Trunk-based development means tiny, frequent merges
cards.hook: Everyone commits to main at least once a day, with unfinished features hidden behind flags instead of living on a long branch.
cards.body: Branches live hours, not weeks, and every commit on main is potentially releasable.

cards.heading: GitFlow's structure has a real cost
cards.hook: Three permanent branch types (main, develop, release) make versioned releases explicit but create frequent merge conflicts and long-lived branches.
cards.body: It fits versioned libraries and mobile apps more than continuously-deployed web services.

cards.heading: A commit format that writes your changelog for you
cards.hook: type(scope): description, with a ! marking a breaking change, is structured enough for tooling to auto-generate changelogs and semantic version bumps.

cards.heading: Never rebase a branch someone else is pulling from
cards.hook: Rebase rewrites commit history — do it freely on your own unpushed branch, never on a shared one, or everyone else's history silently diverges from yours.

cards.heading: PR size is the single biggest predictor of review quality
cards.hook: Reviews on PRs over 400 lines tend to get rubber-stamped — reviewers skim instead of actually reading.
cards.body: Splitting a migration, the logic change, and the tests into separate PRs keeps each one genuinely reviewable.

cards.heading: URLs are nouns, HTTP methods are verbs
cards.hook: POST /createOrder fights the protocol — POST /orders lets the method itself carry the action, which is what makes a REST API predictable to a stranger.

cards.heading: Never return 200 with an error in the body
cards.hook: Status 200 with { error: 'not found' } in the body breaks every monitoring tool and HTTP client that trusts the status code — use the real 404.

cards.heading: A stable error shape is part of the contract
cards.hook: A machine-readable code, a human message, and a requestId for log correlation turn an error response into something a client can actually branch logic on.

cards.heading: Cursor pagination beats offset at scale
cards.hook: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40 breaks the moment a row is inserted mid-pagination — a cursor encoding the last seen id doesn't, and needs no COUNT(*) either.

cards.heading: Idempotency keys stop a retry from duplicating an order
cards.hook: A client-generated key lets the server recognize a retried POST and return the original response instead of creating a second order.

cards.heading: Breaking changes need a new version, additive ones don't
cards.hook: Removing a field, renaming one, or adding a required field all break existing clients — adding an optional field or a new endpoint never does.

cards.heading: Opaque IDs beat sequential integers
cards.hook: ord_abc123 reveals nothing about row count or creation order — a sequential integer lets a competitor estimate your order volume just by watching ids increment.

cards.heading: Code review's real job is knowledge sharing
cards.hook: Catching bugs matters, but the bigger payoff is that everyone ends up understanding more of the codebase than just the part they wrote.

cards.heading: Prefix feedback so the author knows what to do with it
cards.hook: [blocking], [suggestion], [nit], and [question] tell the author at a glance whether a comment must be fixed or is just worth discussing.

cards.heading: Automate the stuff you keep commenting on
cards.hook: If you're leaving comments about semicolons or import order, that's a linter configuration gap, not a review finding.

cards.heading: Rubber-stamping is a PR-size problem, not a discipline problem
cards.hook: Reviews under 50 lines catch the most defects; past 400 lines, reviewers start skimming — the fix is smaller PRs, not stricter reviewers.

cards.heading: Distinguish dictating from suggesting
cards.hook: 'Change this to use a Map' creates friction. 'A Map might be cleaner here since we're doing frequent lookups — thoughts?' starts a conversation instead.

cards.heading: A self-review checklist catches what a second pair of eyes shouldn't have to
cards.hook: Reading your own diff top to bottom before requesting review catches leftover debug logs, TODOs, and commented-out code before anyone else has to.

cards.heading: Protobuf is binary and 3 to 10x smaller than the same data in JSON
cards.hook: That's also why gRPC skips the JSON parsing step entirely — there's no string to parse, just a compact binary layout.

cards.heading: gRPC has four streaming modes REST has none of
cards.hook: Unary, server streaming, client streaming, and bidirectional streaming are all native to gRPC over HTTP/2 — REST's closest equivalent is bolting on WebSockets.

cards.heading: A .proto file is a contract REST usually only has by convention
cards.hook: Protobuf validates field names and types at compile time — most REST APIs ship with no formal schema at all, so a typo in a field name is a runtime surprise instead of a build error.

cards.heading: gRPC can't talk to a browser directly
cards.hook: Binary framing over HTTP/2 isn't something a browser can read — gRPC-Web needs a proxy in between, which is REST's biggest practical advantage for anything public-facing.

cards.heading: The pragmatic answer is usually both
cards.hook: REST at the edge for browsers and third parties, gRPC internally between services you control — a gRPC Gateway can even expose one gRPC service as both at once.

cards.heading: Backpressure is what happens when a producer outruns a consumer
cards.hook: A fast publisher and a slow worker with no flow control between them means the buffer grows until the process runs out of memory.

cards.heading: A write() return value is Node's own backpressure signal
cards.hook: When a writable stream's internal buffer fills, write() returns false — ignoring that and pushing more anyway is exactly how userland buffering replaces the mechanism meant to prevent it.
cards.code:
const ok = writable.write(chunk);
if (!ok) await new Promise(r => writable.once('drain', r));

cards.heading: prefetch is the real flow control knob in a queue consumer
cards.hook: Without it, RabbitMQ pushes every queued message to a consumer at once — prefetch(5) caps how many unacknowledged messages it'll hold in memory at a time.

cards.heading: Acking before processing loses messages on a crash
cards.hook: Ack only after the work actually succeeds — ack first and crash mid-task, and that message is gone forever instead of retried.

cards.heading: A dead letter queue is where messages go to be inspected, not retried forever
cards.hook: Routing a permanently-broken message to a DLQ stops it looping back into the main queue indefinitely.

cards.heading: Counters only go up, gauges go up and down
cards.hook: A request counter resets on restart and only climbs — a gauge for active connections or memory usage reflects the current state at any instant.

cards.heading: A trace follows one request across every service it touches
cards.hook: Each span records one operation's timing and tags; nested spans within a trace reconstruct exactly which hop in a four-service call chain was actually slow.

cards.heading: High-cardinality labels quietly break your metrics backend
cards.hook: Tagging a metric with a raw userId creates one time series per user — millions of them. Tagging with a tier like 'premium' stays a handful of series no matter how many users you have.

cards.heading: Not every failure throws an exception
cards.hook: A slow query or a silently degrading downstream API never raises an error — APM tooling catches these by watching latency and transaction health, not just exception counts.

cards.heading: A correlation id turns a log search into a filter
cards.hook: Attach one id to every log line a single request produces, and 'what happened for this one failed request' becomes one query instead of guessing which interleaved lines belong together.

cards.heading: Synthetic monitoring tests the user journey before a user does
cards.hook: A scripted login-then-checkout flow run every sixty seconds catches a broken critical path minutes before a real customer hits it.

cards.heading: Anomaly detection compares now against your own recent baseline
cards.hook: Error rate at 2x baseline or traffic dropped 70% below it triggers an alert — no hardcoded threshold needed, since what's normal shifts with time of day and season.

cards.heading: Auto-remediation should only do what you'd confidently do yourself at 3am
cards.hook: Clearing a cache or killing idle DB connections is safe to automate; a full service restart is usually gated behind human approval for good reason.

cards.heading: A deployment safety check can catch a bad release before users do
cards.hook: Automatically comparing error rate and p95 latency before and after a deploy is what turns 'users reported it broken' into 'we rolled it back in two minutes.'

cards.heading: Partition tolerance was never actually optional
cards.hook: The real CAP choice only exists during a network partition — and partitions aren't a maybe, they're a when, so every distributed system eventually has to pick CP or AP.

cards.heading: PACELC asks the question CAP leaves out
cards.hook: CAP only covers behavior during a partition — PACELC adds: even with no partition at all, you're still trading consistency against latency, because real consistency needs coordination.

cards.heading: Split brain is what happens when both halves think they're in charge
cards.hook: A network partition convinces each side it's the only surviving system — both start accepting writes, and reconciling the conflict afterward is the hard part quorum-based writes exist to avoid.

cards.heading: The right answer often differs by data type, not by system
cards.hook: A single e-commerce app can run AP for its shopping cart and CP for checkout — CAP is a per-data-type decision, not a single label stamped on the whole architecture.

cards.heading: Read-your-writes is the consistency users actually notice
cards.hook: A user whose own profile edit seems to vanish on refresh will file a bug report — reading from the node they just wrote to fixes exactly that complaint.

cards.heading: Vector clocks detect a conflict without needing synchronized clocks
cards.hook: Two writes with vector clocks that don't dominate each other happened concurrently — no wall-clock timestamp needed, which matters since clocks drift and NTP can even step backward.

cards.heading: Last-write-wins is simple and silently throws data away
cards.hook: Picking the later timestamp as the winner means the losing write just disappears — fine for a view counter, a real problem for two people editing the same document.

cards.heading: CRDTs resolve conflicts with math instead of app logic
cards.hook: A grow-only counter merges by taking the max of each node's count — no custom conflict handler needed, and the merge is mathematically guaranteed to converge.

cards.heading: W + R > N is the formula behind tunable consistency
cards.hook: With 3 replicas, write-quorum 2 and read-quorum 2 guarantees a read always overlaps the latest write — drop either number and you trade consistency for speed.

cards.heading: 2PC's coordinator crash is the scenario that kills it
cards.hook: If the coordinator dies between every participant voting yes and sending commit, every participant sits there holding its locks with no one left to tell it what to do.

cards.heading: A saga trades one big transaction for a chain of small ones
cards.hook: Each service commits its own local transaction and publishes an event; if a later step fails, compensating transactions walk backward undoing what already happened.

cards.heading: Choreography sagas have no bottleneck — and no clear picture either
cards.hook: Services coordinate purely through events with nobody in charge, which scales beautifully until you need to answer 'where exactly did this order get stuck.'

cards.heading: A compensating transaction undoes the effect, not the history
cards.hook: You can't un-charge a credit card — refunding it achieves the same semantic outcome without pretending the original charge never happened.

cards.heading: TCC adds a reservation step sagas skip entirely
cards.hook: Try reserves resources without committing, Confirm commits only if every try succeeded, Cancel releases the reservation otherwise — better isolation than a saga, at the cost of every service needing to support all three verbs.

cards.heading: A fencing token stops a lock holder that doesn't know it's expired
cards.hook: A GC pause can make a process believe it still holds a lock long after it expired — tagging every write with a monotonically increasing token lets storage reject the stale one even if two holders overlap.

cards.heading: ZooKeeper's sequential ephemeral nodes make locking fair
cards.hook: Whoever created the lowest-numbered node holds the lock; everyone else watches only the node directly ahead of them, so there's no thundering herd when the lock is released.

cards.heading: An epoch number is what stops a demoted leader from still acting
cards.hook: If a leader with epoch 5 gets partitioned and a new leader is elected at epoch 6, storage simply rejects any write still tagged epoch 5 once the partition heals.

cards.heading: Check-then-act is a race condition with a SQL query
cards.hook: if balance >= 100 then deduct(100) leaves a gap where two concurrent requests both pass the check and both deduct — a single conditional UPDATE closes that gap atomically.
cards.code:
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100
WHERE id = 123 AND balance >= 100;

cards.heading: Raft traded Paxos's complexity for an explicit leader
cards.hook: All writes go through one elected leader who replicates to followers — simpler to reason about than Paxos, which is why etcd and Consul both chose it.

cards.heading: Exactly-once delivery is a myth — exactly-once processing isn't
cards.hook: A broker can never fully distinguish 'message lost' from 'ack lost', so true exactly-once delivery is impossible — what you actually build is at-least-once delivery plus an idempotent, deduplicated consumer.

cards.heading: The transactional outbox pattern closes the dual-write gap
cards.hook: Writing to your own table and publishing an event in the same database transaction guarantees the event is never lost even if the message broker is down at that exact moment.

cards.heading: Kafka only orders messages within a partition
cards.hook: Pick the partition key carefully — all of one user's orders landing in the same partition keeps them ordered, but a poorly chosen key creates one overloaded hot partition.

cards.heading: Causal ordering only constrains what's actually related
cards.hook: If a comment depends on a post, every node must see the post first — but two unrelated posts from different people can arrive in any order without anyone noticing.

cards.heading: A hybrid logical clock looks like wall time but behaves like a logical one
cards.hook: It combines physical time with a logical counter so it tracks causality correctly without needing perfectly synchronized clocks across every node.

cards.heading: The distributed monolith is the worst outcome, not the middle ground
cards.hook: Services that must deploy together or share one database get every operational cost of microservices with none of the independence that was supposed to justify it.

cards.heading: Under ten developers, a monolith is usually more productive
cards.hook: The coordination overhead of separate deployments and cross-service debugging costs more than it buys until you actually have multiple teams stepping on each other.

cards.heading: The strangler fig pattern migrates a monolith without a rewrite
cards.hook: New functionality goes straight into services; old functionality gets extracted one capability at a time, routed over, and deleted from the monolith — never a big-bang cutover.

cards.heading: Conway's Law isn't a suggestion, it's a prediction
cards.hook: Organize teams by business capability and services end up cleanly bounded; organize by technical layer instead and the services will mirror that same awkward split.

cards.heading: Decentralized data ownership is what makes a service actually independent
cards.hook: The moment two services share one database, neither can change its schema without coordinating with the other — that's the tightest coupling microservices exist to avoid.

cards.heading: A bounded context is where a word means one specific thing
cards.hook: 'Customer' in the sales context and 'Customer' in support might share a name but have completely different attributes — the boundary is exactly where that meaning changes.

cards.heading: Chatty services are a boundary problem wearing a performance costume
cards.hook: If completing one operation means five synchronous round trips between two services, the real fix usually isn't caching — it's that the boundary split apart things that belong together.

cards.heading: Event storming finds boundaries by following what actually happens
cards.hook: Lay out every domain event in the order they occur, and bounded contexts reveal themselves as the natural clusters instead of being guessed at upfront.

cards.heading: An anti-corruption layer keeps someone else's model out of your domain
cards.hook: A legacy system that calls users CUST_REC doesn't get to dictate your vocabulary — the layer translates at the boundary so your own domain model stays clean.

cards.heading: It's easier to merge two services than to split one wrong
cards.hook: Start coarser than you think you need. A boundary drawn too early, before the domain is understood, costs far more to unwind than two slightly-too-big services cost to eventually split.

cards.heading: A gateway should route and enforce policy, never hold business logic
cards.hook: The moment a gateway starts making domain decisions instead of just authenticating, rate-limiting, and forwarding, you've built a second place business rules can silently diverge.

cards.heading: A service mesh buys you mTLS and retries with zero app code changes
cards.hook: Sidecar proxies handle encryption, circuit breaking, and traffic shifting at the infrastructure layer — but only worth the operational overhead past roughly twenty services.

cards.heading: A stateless instance is safe to kill at any second
cards.hook: Session data in Redis instead of process memory, uploads streamed straight to S3 instead of local disk — any instance can then handle any request, and a crash loses nothing.

cards.heading: CQRS splits the model that writes from the model that reads
cards.hook: The command side validates and emits events; the query side just serves denormalized, pre-joined views — worth the extra complexity only when read and write need very different shapes.

cards.heading: BFF trades code duplication for a perfectly-shaped API per client
cards.hook: A mobile app and a web dashboard often want wildly different slices of the same data — a backend-for-frontend per client type avoids both over-fetching and under-fetching for either.

cards.heading: Client-side and server-side discovery move the same decision to different places
cards.hook: Client-side discovery puts load-balancing logic in every client language you support; server-side puts it behind one load balancer that becomes the single hop everyone pays.

cards.heading: Dynamic secrets limit the blast radius of a leak
cards.hook: A database credential generated on demand with a short TTL is useless to an attacker an hour after it leaks — a credential that never expires is useful forever.

cards.heading: Most feature flags are meant to die young
cards.hook: A release flag should be deleted the moment the feature fully ships — the ones worth keeping long-term are the operational kill-switches and permission gates, not the ones gating last quarter's launch.

cards.heading: A missing config value should crash the process at boot, not mid-request
cards.hook: Validating required configuration keys on startup turns a three-hours-later production incident into an immediate, obvious deploy failure.

cards.heading: Least connections beats round robin when request duration varies
cards.hook: Round robin assumes every request takes the same time — route to whichever instance has the fewest active connections instead, and a few slow requests stop silently piling onto one unlucky instance.

cards.heading: Expansion and contraction is how you rename a field with zero downtime
cards.hook: Add the new field alongside the old one, write and read both, migrate every client over, and only then delete the old field — skip straight to renaming and you break whoever hasn't deployed yet.

cards.heading: Protobuf's field numbers are the real identifier, not the names
cards.hook: Renaming a field is safe; reusing a deleted field's number for something new is not — mark it reserved instead, or an old client reads the new field as if it were the old one.

cards.heading: Semantic versioning tells consumers the blast radius before they read the changelog
cards.hook: Major means something broke, minor means something was safely added, patch means a bug got fixed — that discipline is what lets automated tooling decide safely whether to auto-upgrade.

cards.heading: A read projection can always be thrown away and rebuilt
cards.hook: Since it's just a replay of the event log, a buggy projection isn't a data-loss incident — delete it, replay from the beginning, and the correct version comes back.

cards.heading: Structure by business capability, not by technical role
cards.hook: A controllers/services/models split describes the framework, not the product — a folder per business capability means changing 'how orders work' never touches an unrelated folder.

cards.heading: Three layers map onto the actual request flow
cards.hook: Entry-point adapts the external payload, domain holds the real business logic in plain objects, data-access is the only layer allowed near the database — every request visits all three, in that order.

cards.heading: Wrap third-party libraries behind your own package
cards.hook: If every component imports a logging library directly, swapping it later means touching every component — wrap it in an internal package once, and only the wrapper changes.

cards.heading: TypeScript bundles two different offerings people conflate
cards.hook: Type safety and OOP design constructs (abstract classes, decorators) are separate choices — teams that adopt TypeScript purely for type safety often end up reaching for class hierarchies just because the tool is sitting there.

cards.heading: Throwing a string instead of an Error throws away the stack trace
cards.hook: throw 'something broke' has no stack trace, fails instanceof Error checks, and gives every catch block a different shape to guess at — always throw a real Error.

cards.heading: isOperational is the one flag that decides crash or continue
cards.hook: An expected failure — bad input, a timeout — should log and keep serving; a programmer bug leaves the process in an unknown state and should restart, not limp along.

cards.heading: return somePromise() silently drops a stack frame
cards.hook: V8's async stack traces only extend across an actual await — a bare return of a promise without awaiting it means the function that returned it is simply missing from the eventual stack trace.

cards.heading: unhandledRejection is a safety net, not a strategy
cards.hook: A forgotten .catch makes a promise rejection vanish silently — Node surfaces a warning, but routing it through the same centralized handler as every other error is what actually catches it.

cards.heading: One ErrorHandler, called from every entry point
cards.hook: Express middleware, cron jobs, and queue consumers all funneling into the same handler means a failure gets logged and classified the same way no matter where it originated.

cards.heading: There's no safe way to resume after an uncaught exception
cards.hook: A singleton that lost internal state mid-operation can't be trusted to keep serving traffic — let a process restarter own recovery instead of trying to swallow the exception and carry on.

cards.heading: ESLint flags problems, Prettier fixes them
cards.hook: They only overlap on formatting rules — running both there causes them to fight each other, so disable ESLint's formatting rules and let Prettier own that slice exclusively.

cards.heading: var leaks outside the block it looks like it belongs to
cards.hook: A for loop using var and a setTimeout inside logs the loop's final value N times, not each iteration's value — let and const are block-scoped and don't have this trap.

cards.heading: Named exports survive a rename, default exports don't
cards.hook: Two files importing the same default export can give it two completely different local names — a named export makes find-all-references and automated renames actually reliable.

cards.heading: Mixing callbacks, .then(), and async/await forces three mental models per file
cards.hook: Standardizing on async/await for new code means every reader parses the same control-flow shape instead of context-switching between three different error-handling conventions.

cards.heading: A good test name is a requirements statement
cards.hook: 'When no price is specified, then the product status is pending approval' tells a reader what broke without opening the test body — 'should return the right status' tells them nothing.

cards.heading: Arrange-Act-Assert gives every test the same predictable shape
cards.hook: A reader can jump straight to the Assert block to see what's actually being verified, instead of parsing setup and verification tangled together.

cards.heading: Shared seed data couples tests that look independent
cards.hook: One test renaming a record from a shared seed file silently breaks a later test that assumed the name was untouched — have every test create exactly the records it needs instead.

cards.heading: A passing response doesn't mean the write actually happened
cards.hook: A handler can return 200 OK while silently failing to persist anything — check the state change, the external call, and the log output, not just the HTTP response.

cards.heading: Binding a fixed port collides the moment tests run in parallel
cards.hook: Let the OS assign an ephemeral port in tests and fix the port only in production — two test workers starting a server on the same hardcoded port is a guaranteed crash.

cards.heading: NODE_ENV=production isn't cosmetic — it roughly doubles throughput
cards.hook: Express and many libraries branch on it to skip debug work and enable view caching; leaving it unset silently runs your production traffic in development mode.

cards.heading: package-lock.json pins the exact tree that passed QA
cards.hook: A loose semver range can silently resolve to a different, untested version on the next install — the lock file is what guarantees prod gets the same dependency tree staging did.

cards.heading: npm ci fails loudly instead of silently drifting
cards.hook: npm install reconciles package.json against the lock file and may update it; npm ci refuses to and errors out the moment the two disagree — exactly the behavior you want in CI.

cards.heading: A stateless instance is a disposable one
cards.hook: Uploaded files on local disk and in-memory sessions die with the instance that held them — externalize both to S3 and Redis, and any instance can be killed and replaced without losing anything.

cards.heading: nginx should serve static files, not Node
cards.hook: Every static asset request competing with API requests for Node's single thread is wasted throughput — nginx's multi-threaded, kernel-level file serving does it without touching the event loop at all.

cards.heading: A transaction id turns 'search every log line' into one filter
cards.hook: AsyncLocalStorage carries a single id through an entire async call chain, so every log line from one request — across every service it touched — shares the same searchable key.

cards.heading: eval on user input is remote code execution, not a bug
cards.hook: If any part of a string reaching eval() or new Function() can be influenced by a request, an attacker has effectively gained arbitrary code execution on your server.

cards.heading: A nested quantifier regex can freeze your entire process
cards.hook: A pattern like (a+)+ against a crafted input can take exponential time on Node's single thread — that's a ReDoS, and it blocks every other request the process is handling while it runs.

cards.heading: Parameterized queries aren't optional, they're the whole defense
cards.hook: String-concatenating user input into a query is the textbook SQL injection — a query builder or ORM that supports parameterized queries by default closes that hole structurally, not by discipline.

cards.heading: Comparing secrets with === leaks them one character at a time
cards.hook: A normal string comparison exits on the first mismatched character — the tiny timing difference between failing at character 1 versus character 20 is enough to reconstruct a secret byte by byte.

cards.heading: Math.random() is fast, predictable, and wrong for tokens
cards.hook: A password-reset code or API key generated with Math.random() is guessable — crypto.randomBytes() draws from the OS's actual entropy source instead.

cards.heading: A stack trace in an HTTP response hands an attacker a map
cards.hook: File paths, dependency versions, and internal logic all leak through a default error handler in anything but production mode — log the full detail server-side, send the client a generic message.

cards.heading: A single synchronous handler stalls every concurrent request
cards.hook: Node runs your JavaScript on one thread — a 30ms busy-loop in one handler doesn't just add 30ms to that request, it adds 30ms to every other request the process happens to be serving at that moment.

cards.heading: fs.readFileSync in a request handler blocks everyone
cards.hook: The sync variant runs entirely on the main thread; the async variant hands the work to libuv's thread pool and frees the event loop while it waits.

cards.heading: worker_threads moves real CPU work off the request path
cards.hook: Image resizing or password hashing run on a separate thread with its own event loop, leaving the main thread free to keep handling requests while the heavy computation happens elsewhere.

cards.heading: A nested find() inside a map() turns O(n) into O(n*m)
cards.hook: Looking up a matching user for every order by scanning the whole users array each time gets quadratic fast — build a Map once, and every lookup afterward is O(1).

cards.heading: Profile before you optimize, because intuition about 'slow' is usually wrong
cards.hook: Flame graph tools show exactly where time actually goes — the function that looks expensive at a glance is rarely the one actually dominating the profile.

cards.heading: A multi-stage build ships only the compiled output, not the toolchain
cards.hook: Compilers, devDependencies, and source files that never get copied into the final stage simply never reach the shipped image — smaller size, smaller attack surface, for free.

cards.heading: Layer order decides what survives the build cache
cards.hook: Copying package.json and running npm ci before copying application code means editing a source file never invalidates the dependency-install layer.

cards.heading: npm start as the container's CMD breaks graceful shutdown
cards.hook: npm doesn't forward SIGTERM to the Node process it spawned — running Node directly as PID 1 means it actually receives the signal orchestrators send on every rolling deploy.

cards.heading: Two memory limits are needed, not one
cards.hook: Without the V8 --max-old-space-size flag, the garbage collector doesn't know to work harder as memory approaches the container's ceiling, and the process can crash using only half the available memory.

cards.heading: Deleting a secret in a later layer doesn't remove it from history
cards.hook: A build ARG for an npm token is still recoverable from the image's layer history even after a later RUN step deletes the file — a BuildKit secret mount never writes it to a layer at all.

cards.heading: A toy service assumes dependencies never fail; production assumes they will
cards.hook: Networks have latency and packet loss, services crash and restart, load spikes unpredictably — reliability patterns exist specifically to bridge that gap between the demo and the real thing.

cards.heading: Slow failures are worse than fast ones
cards.hook: A hung request holds a thread, a connection, and memory indefinitely — failing fast frees those resources immediately for a request that can actually succeed.

cards.heading: A cascading failure follows the same four stages every time
cards.hook: One component degrades, callers exhaust their own resources waiting on it, those callers fail too, and the failure spreads until the whole system is down.

cards.heading: Availability and reliability are improved by different levers
cards.hook: Reliability means failures happen less often — MTBF. Availability means you recover faster when they do — MTTR. A system can be unreliable but highly available if it fails often and recovers in seconds.

cards.heading: Every external call needs a timeout — this is not optional
cards.hook: Without one, a hung request holds a thread or connection indefinitely, and enough of those exhaust the pool and take the whole service down with them.

cards.heading: Naive retries can turn a slow service into a dead one
cards.hook: A slow service under load causes timeouts, timeouts trigger retries, retries add more load, the service gets slower still — that death spiral is exactly why retries need backoff and a budget.

cards.heading: Not every error deserves a retry
cards.hook: A 503 from an overloaded service is worth retrying — a 400 from malformed input will fail identically every single time, and retrying it just wastes a round trip.

cards.heading: Jitter exists to stop a thousand clients from retrying in perfect unison
cards.hook: Without it, every client that timed out at exactly 5 seconds retries at exactly the same moment, overwhelming a service that was just starting to recover.

cards.heading: An idempotency key makes a retried POST safe
cards.hook: The server checks whether it's seen the key before and returns the cached response instead of creating a second order — the client can retry freely without fear of duplicating the side effect.

cards.heading: A circuit breaker has three states, like the electrical kind
cards.hook: Closed lets requests through normally, Open fails every request immediately without even calling the service, Half-Open lets a handful through to test if it's recovered.

cards.heading: Client errors shouldn't trip a circuit breaker
cards.hook: A 404 or a 400 means the request itself was wrong, not that the service is unhealthy — only timeouts, connection errors, and 5xx responses should count toward the failure threshold.

cards.heading: A bulkhead keeps one failing dependency from exhausting everything
cards.hook: Separate connection pools per downstream service mean a slow payment service can only ever consume its own slice of resources, never the pool inventory or shipping also depend on.

cards.heading: A fallback turns an open circuit into a degraded response, not a dead one
cards.hook: Serving a cached result or a default value when the circuit opens means users see slightly stale data instead of a hard failure — degraded beats broken.

cards.heading: Roll a circuit breaker out in observe mode first
cards.hook: Deploy it logging what it would do without actually opening any circuits, tune the thresholds against real traffic, then engage it for real.

cards.heading: Fixed window counters have a boundary bug built in
cards.hook: A hundred requests just before a minute boundary and another hundred just after both pass a 100-per-minute fixed-window limit — 200 requests in two seconds, limit technically never exceeded.

cards.heading: Token bucket is the one that handles bursts gracefully
cards.hook: Tokens refill at a steady rate but the bucket can hold a reserve, so a brief burst spends saved-up tokens instead of getting rejected outright — the standard choice for production rate limiting.

cards.heading: Rejecting some requests fast beats processing all of them slowly
cards.hook: Under real overload, serving 70% of requests well is a better outcome for users than serving 100% of them so slowly that most time out anyway.

cards.heading: Priority-based shedding protects checkout before it protects recommendations
cards.hook: When a system sheds load, dropping low-value requests first — analytics, recommendations — keeps the operations that actually matter running.

cards.heading: Backpressure is cooperative, load shedding is defensive
cards.hook: Backpressure asks an upstream producer to slow down — load shedding just rejects requests outright. Use backpressure between your own internal services, load shedding at the edge facing external clients.

cards.heading: Liveness and readiness ask two different questions
cards.hook: Liveness asks 'should this process be restarted' — readiness asks 'should this instance receive traffic right now.' Conflating them means a slow database takes down instances that were actually fine.

cards.heading: Separating the two probes avoids a restart loop
cards.hook: If the database goes down and liveness includes a DB check, the orchestrator restarts every instance — the new ones can't reach the DB either, so they get restarted too, forever.

cards.heading: SIGKILL can't be caught — SIGTERM is the one you have to handle
cards.hook: An orchestrator sends SIGTERM with a grace period before escalating to SIGKILL; a process that doesn't listen for SIGTERM drops every in-flight request the moment that grace period expires.

cards.heading: Stop accepting new work before draining what's in flight
cards.hook: Close the listening port first, then wait for active requests to finish within a bounded timeout, then close database and queue connections — in that order, not all at once.

cards.heading: A health check that queries the database on every ping can overwhelm it
cards.hook: Caching the result for a few seconds means a load balancer checking every instance every five seconds doesn't itself become meaningful load on the dependency being checked.

cards.heading: Authentication asks who you are, authorization asks what you can do
cards.hook: Conflating the two in code is how a system ends up checking identity in the same place it checks permissions — keep them as genuinely separate concerns.

cards.heading: The Authorization Code flow never exposes the token to the browser
cards.hook: The client exchanges a short-lived code for the access token via a backend call — the Implicit flow skipped that step and put the token straight in the URL, which is exactly why it's deprecated.

cards.heading: A JWT is signed, not encrypted — anyone can read the payload
cards.hook: Base64 is not encryption; decoding a JWT's payload is one line of code for anyone who intercepts it, so never put a password or anything sensitive inside the claims.

cards.heading: Validate the algorithm, not just the signature
cards.hook: An attacker who knows a service expects RS256 can craft an HS256 token using the public key as the HMAC secret — explicitly checking the algorithm matches what's expected closes that specific forgery.

cards.heading: mTLS makes both sides of a connection prove who they are
cards.hook: Regular TLS only has the server present a certificate — mutual TLS has the client present one too, which is why service meshes use it for service-to-service authentication with no shared secret anywhere.
